records.sourceFile: Sports injuries and game stakes - Concussions in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Courty P, Cisyk J. Sports injuries and game stakes: Concussions in the National Football League. Economic Inquiry. 2023.
paper.abstract: NFL regular-season games differ in importance for playoff qualification. The authors build an incentive-based measure of how a win changes a team's qualification probability and relate it to concussions. Teams were 24 percentage points more likely to suffer a concussion in games where a win secures a playoff berth.
paper.tldr: Concussion risk in NFL games appears higher when a win would secure playoff qualification. This is an observational finding from one league, so it should prompt readiness for high-stakes games rather than a firm risk estimate.
paper.methods: Team-game panel of NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015, excluding neutral-site games and each team's final game (1896 observations; 1282 in a restricted sample meeting the approximation conditions). A swing measure of playoff odds was computed for each game, concussion events were taken from injury reports, and linear probability models included team, season and game fixed effects and game-condition controls, with standard errors clustered by team.
paper.findings: The swing variable had a positive association with concussion incidence that reached the 5 or 10 percent significance level once team or season fixed effects were included (coefficients about 0.24 to 0.31 with controls). In-sample, a 40 percentage point swing was linked to about a 10 percentage point higher chance of at least one concussion, from a base of about 25 percent, and the authors extrapolate to 24 percentage points for a swing of one. Artificial turf was linked to 6 to 7 points higher risk, and some alternative swing definitions gave weaker or non-significant results.
paper.limitations: Observational design with no direct measure of game intensity or exposure. The stakes measure depends on a model of playoff odds, and the 24 point figure lies outside the observed swing range. Injury data come from public reports, and the findings are limited to NFL regular-season games from 2012 to 2015.
paper.practicalImplications: Concussion risk may rise in games where the stakes are high, so staff could plan extra sideline and concussion-protocol readiness for those games. The paper does not test any prevention measure.
paper.athleteDev: This paper does not address athlete development or performance. It covers injury risk linked to game stakes only.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return to sport. It measures how often concussions occur in high-stakes games and says nothing about recovery time or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Sprinting and hamstring strain injury - Beliefs and practices of professional physical performance coaches in Australian football.pdf

paper.citation: Freeman BW, Talpey SW, James LP, Young WB. Sprinting and hamstring strain injury: Beliefs and practices of professional physical performance coaches in Australian football. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2021;48:12-19.
paper.abstract: This survey asked high-performance managers at Australian Football League clubs about their beliefs and practices for sprinting and hamstring strain injury. Nine of 18 invited managers responded. Sprinting, eccentric strength training and periodisation were seen as effective, and all coaches reported regular sprint exposure, but the speed thresholds they used for sprinting varied widely.
paper.tldr: Nine AFL high-performance managers said sprinting and eccentric hamstring training help prevent hamstring injury, and all reported regular sprint exposure. Their definitions of sprinting speed varied widely, and GPS was the main tool for tracking maximum speed.
paper.methods: An online, Delphi-validated questionnaire was sent to 18 AFL high-performance managers between November 2019 and February 2020. It used closed and open questions about beliefs, training practices and speed thresholds. Two researchers coded the open responses into themes.
paper.findings: Nine of 18 managers responded, and all nine rated acceleration and maximum-speed sprinting as common or very common HSI activities. All used weekly eccentric hamstring strength testing and reported sprint training, while sprinting was defined as anything from above 85% to above 95% of maximum velocity. No respondent reported measuring sprinting faster than 85% of maximum velocity, and GPS was the main way maximum speed was tested (nine in the results, eight of nine in the discussion).
paper.limitations: Small sample from one league (9 of 18 invited, all male), with anonymous self-report that may reflect response bias. Respondents were asked only about AFL experience, and the study did not compare coach beliefs with injury data. The count of coaches testing maximum speed with GPS differs between the results (n = 9) and the discussion (8 of 9).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can check whether the speed thresholds they use match how they define sprinting, since the most common definition of sprinting was above 90% of maximum velocity (5 of 9) but none reported measuring it above 85%. The survey does not show which sprint dose prevents HSI, so it supports reviewing thresholds and monitoring exposure rather than adopting a set dose.
paper.athleteDev: Define sprint exposure with relative speed bands, such as a percentage of each athlete's maximum velocity, and make sure the bands used to prescribe and monitor sprinting match the definition the staff uses. Six of nine respondents said the sprint dose should be individualised to each athlete.
paper.rtp: This survey cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes coach beliefs about prevention and training, not rehabilitation progression or readiness criteria for athletes returning from HSI.

records.sourceFile: Squatting Biomechanics After Femoroacetabular Impingement Surgery - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Generoso TO, Pelegrinelli ARM, Gonzalez FF, Pallone LV, Locks R, Guadagnin EC, et al. Squatting Biomechanics After Femoroacetabular Impingement Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Clin J Sport Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 3D squat biomechanics studies of patients who had hip impingement surgery, comparing each patient before and after surgery. Most studies found no significant change in kinematics or kinetics, while a few individual studies reported changes in squat depth, pelvic motion and hip or knee flexion.
paper.tldr: Across six before-and-after studies of hip impingement surgery, squat mechanics changed little on average. Bone deformity alone may not explain the squat limits seen in these patients.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided search of six databases (last searched 12 December 2024) for 3D motion-analysis studies that compared the same FAI patients before and after surgery during squatting. Study quality was rated with MINORS, and five studies were pooled with random-effects models for seven kinematic outcomes. Where study populations overlapped, the study with the higher MINORS score was used.
paper.findings: Six studies were reviewed, with 74 presurgical and 73 postsurgical patients tested 6 to 32 months after surgery, and the pooled analysis showed no significant pre- to post-surgery differences in the kinematic measures. Individual studies reported greater squat depth in one study, greater pelvic sagittal range of motion in another, and opposite changes in anterior pelvic tilt between two studies. Kinetic findings were inconsistent across the four studies that reported them.
paper.limitations: Few studies and patients, with three studies drawing on one cohort, which limits the pooled estimates. Kinematic processing and data reporting differed between studies, most were case-control or cross-sectional with moderate quality, and participants came from orthopaedic clinics. Table 2 gives squat depth as a percentage of leg length without stating which direction means deeper, so Lamontagne 2011's lower postoperative value is hard to reconcile with the reported greater depth.
paper.practicalImplications: Surgery alone did not reliably change squat mechanics on average, so staff should not assume that a squat pattern normalises after bone correction. The authors suggest that muscle-balance and rehabilitation work may influence outcomes, but the review did not test rehabilitation effects directly.
paper.athleteDev: Do not assume that squat depth, pelvic motion or squat speed improve after hip impingement surgery. Assess squat mechanics after surgery rather than relying on the procedure to restore them. The evidence comes from clinical patients, so it does not set athlete loading or performance targets.
paper.rtp: The review gives only a general picture: squat depth and motion patterns changed little on average 6 to 32 months after surgery. It cannot set return-to-sport or squat clearance criteria, because it did not study athletes or sport-specific tasks.

records.sourceFile: Stingers—A Review of Current Understanding and Management.pdf

paper.citation: Gebeyehu TF, Harrop JS, Dian JA, Matsoukas S, Vaccaro AR. Stingers - A Review of Current Understanding and Management. Applied Sciences. 2025;15:3510.
paper.abstract: A narrative review of stingers, the brief loss of function in one arm after a stretch or compression injury to the brachial plexus or cervical nerve roots. It covers pathology, clinical features, imaging, electrodiagnostics, treatment, rehabilitation and return to play, and the authors rate all the literature reviewed as level IV and V evidence.
paper.tldr: Most stingers are mild and clear within minutes, and conservative care usually works. Return to play rests largely on expert opinion, with symptom duration, repeat episodes and imaging guiding decisions. Surgery is rare and reserved for severe nerve root or nerve injury.
paper.methods: Narrative review. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for 'stingers' and 'burners' without Boolean operators, with title screening and a focus on English-language literature from the past five years, supplemented by reference lists and older foundational work. Sources included case reports, reviews, retrospective and prospective studies, expert opinion (including a modified Delphi consensus) and book chapters.
paper.findings: Stingers accounted for 62.2% of NFL neck injuries in one study, and 50.3% of football players reported a lifetime stinger in a survey. In the Delphi consensus cited, 69.9% of spine surgeons agreed that first-time stingers under 5 minutes need no imaging, and 84.5% agreed imaging is indicated if symptoms last over 5 minutes or recur. Surgery is reserved for grade IIIA and IIIB injuries, and the review states that its timing and type remain unsettled.
paper.limitations: The authors state the review is not systematic and does not cover all the literature. All the evidence reviewed is level IV and V, and incidence data are missing for sports such as MMA, judo and weightlifting. The 84.5% Delphi figure is used for two different statements (imaging after 5 minutes in section 8; same-day return without MRI in section 10), so check the source before citing it.
paper.practicalImplications: For a first stinger that clears within five minutes, with full pain-free neck and shoulder motion and no weakness or sensory change, the review cites expert agreement for same-day return without imaging. Repeat episodes or symptoms lasting longer than five minutes call for imaging and serial examination. Staff should test the brachial plexus muscles in detail, not only grip strength, and rule out spinal cord or vascular injury before anything else.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review's prevention points: avoid clothesline and spear tackling, use protective equipment such as a cowboy collar, restore neck motion, and strengthen the neck and shoulder girdle. Shoulder pad fit may matter, since one cited study linked pads to compression at Erb's point during tackling. The review gives no training dose or load guidance.
paper.rtp: Return to play follows expert consensus. A first stinger with symptoms clearing within five minutes and no strength, sensory or range-of-motion loss is cited as a same-day return, while repeat or prolonged episodes need imaging and serial examination. Grade IIIA or IIIB injury is an absolute contraindication to return, and the authors lean toward MRI for every episode regardless of symptom duration.

records.sourceFile: Stretch imposed on active muscle elicits positive adaptations in strain risk factors and exercise-induced muscle damage.pdf

paper.citation: Kay AD, Rubley B, Talbot C, Mina M, Baross AW, Blazevich AJ. Stretch imposed on active muscle elicits positive adaptations in strain risk factors and exercise-induced muscle damage. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2018.
paper.abstract: Six weeks of twice-weekly stretches imposed on maximally contracted knee extensors (isokinetic eccentric contractions) in 26 recreationally active adults increased eccentric strength, range of motion, stretch tolerance, elastic energy storage, muscle thickness, pennation angle and tendon stiffness, and reduced the CK response and soreness after a downhill run.
paper.tldr: Six weeks of maximal eccentric stretches on the knee extensors improved range, stretch tolerance, strength and some damage markers in recreationally active adults. The study measured risk factors in healthy people, not injury rates.
paper.methods: Randomized controlled trial with 13 participants in each group, matched by sex. The experimental group did five sets of 12 three-second maximal isokinetic eccentric knee extensor contractions (0 to 90 degrees, 30 degrees per second), twice weekly for 6 weeks, on both legs. Before and after training, range of motion, passive and active moments, ultrasound measures of vastus lateralis architecture and tendon stiffness, serum CK and DOMS were measured, with a 20-minute downhill run used to provoke muscle damage.
paper.findings: In the experimental group, knee flexion range of motion increased by 5.2 degrees, peak passive moment by 55.4% and elastic energy storage by 73.0%. Isometric and eccentric knee extensor moments rose 17.4% and 29.5%. Vastus lateralis thickness rose 7.8%, pennation angle 9.0% and tendon stiffness 8.7%, while passive muscle-tendon stiffness fell 9.4% (not significant). The CK increase after the downhill run was smaller after training (46.0%) than before (107.6%), and knee extensor DOMS was absent or minimal after training. The control group showed no significant change in the mechanical, strength or architecture measures, and its CK rise after the downhill run was similar before (115.4%) and after (120.5%) the 6 weeks.
paper.limitations: The number of participants was small, and the outcome measures were single laboratory tests. DOMS was only ranked for presence and severity across muscle groups, not scored on a scale. Fascicle strain during stretch was not measured, and tendon stiffness may be underestimated because knee movement was not corrected for. The abstract reports a CK change of -70.0%, but the results section reports -70.4%. Injury incidence was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In recreationally active adults, a 6-week program of maximal eccentric knee extensor stretches improved range, strength and muscle-damage responses in the trained muscle. Staff could consider this approach for knee extensors in similar groups, but not as proof of injury prevention.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The program increased eccentric strength and tendon stiffness in the trained muscle, which the authors consider functionally important for athletic tasks. The paper does not test athletes or sport performance, so the link to sport performance is an inference.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used to set return-to-sport loading. It tested healthy recreationally active adults with no recent injury and measured no injured participants or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Subsequent musculoskeletal injury after concussion in National Football League players.pdf

paper.citation: Wasserman EB, Chretien A, Harmon KG, Putukian M, Okonkwo D, Solomon GS, et al. Subsequent musculoskeletal injury after concussion in National Football League players. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: In a retrospective cohort of NFL players from 2015 to 2021, the authors compared the hazard of subsequent time-loss lower extremity or any musculoskeletal injury after concussion with non-concussed players in the same game and with players returning from an upper extremity injury. Neither comparison showed a statistically significant difference, and the authors suggest that deconditioning or other factors linked to lost participation time may explain the higher injury risk seen after concussion in some settings.
paper.tldr: Among NFL players, a concussion did not significantly raise the risk of later musculoskeletal injury over the season after adjustment for prior injuries. The authors suggest time away from sport, rather than the concussion itself, may be what matters, but they did not measure deconditioning.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort from the NFL electronic health record (2015 to 2021 preseason and regular season). Concussed players were compared with two groups: all non-concussed players from the same game, and players with a time-loss upper extremity injury. Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for prior injuries, prior concussions, tenure and roster position, with follow-up measured in player-plays and sensitivity analyses at 30 and 60 days.
paper.findings: Compared with non-concussed players in the same game, the adjusted hazard of time-loss lower extremity injury was 1.09 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.35) over the season and 1.12 (0.90 to 1.41) when days missed were included; for any time-loss musculoskeletal injury it was 1.06 (0.88 to 1.27) and 1.08 (0.89 to 1.31). At 30 days without days-missed adjustment, hazards were significantly higher (lower extremity 1.39, 1.07 to 1.82; any injury 1.36, 1.08 to 1.70) but not once days missed were included. Compared with upper extremity injury, season hazards were 0.78 (0.60 to 1.02) for lower extremity and 0.82 (0.65 to 1.04) for any musculoskeletal injury, with a significantly lower lower extremity hazard at 60 days (0.74, 0.56 to 0.98).
paper.limitations: Men in one elite league, so findings may not transfer to women, other sports, or non-elite players. Follow-up was censored at the end of the season or roster removal, prior injury history before the NFL was not available, and rookies were excluded. The authors could not measure deconditioning, and the comparison groups differ in the time they spend at risk after an injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat the time lost after a concussion as a reason for a structured, progressive conditioning plan before full return. The same plan is worth considering after any upper extremity injury that keeps an athlete out of sport. The study did not find extra musculoskeletal risk after concussion compared with other injured players, but it cannot rule out a modest increase.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Keep a player's physical conditioning up during any time away from sport, and plan the return with a graded build-up, since the authors suggest time lost, rather than the concussion itself, may drive later injury risk.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study supports a rigorous, staged return to sport after concussion and after an upper extremity injury, and it suggests that time lost is a key risk factor. It does not establish that a particular return protocol reduces injury, and the authors call for further research on that question.

records.sourceFile: Sudden cardiac death in young athletes - JACC State of the Art Review.pdf

paper.citation: Finocchiaro G, Westaby J, Sheppard MN, Papadakis M, Sharma S. Sudden Cardiac Death in Young Athletes: JACC State-of-the-Art Review. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(2):350-370.
paper.abstract: This state-of-the-art review covers the epidemiology and causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, including cardiomyopathies, channelopathies and coronary anomalies. It also addresses the difficulty of separating the athlete's heart from disease, preparticipation screening, resuscitation, and shared decision making about exercise when a cardiac condition is found.
paper.tldr: Sudden cardiac death in young athletes is rare but usually linked to an inherited heart condition or coronary anomaly that was not detected beforehand. A cardiac diagnosis does not automatically end sport, and decisions should follow expert assessment and shared decision making.
paper.methods: Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search method is described. The authors draw on incidence studies, national registries, autopsy series and guideline statements from the United States, Europe and elsewhere, and summarise Table 2 comparing AHA/ACC and ESC recommendations for sports participation.
paper.findings: Reported incidence of sudden cardiac death in young athletes varies widely, from 0.24 per 100,000 athlete-years in Minnesota high school athletes to 6.8 per 100,000 athlete-years in a screened UK adolescent football cohort. Inherited cardiac conditions (cardiomyopathies and channelopathies) and congenital coronary artery anomalies are the most common causes, and a structurally normal heart at autopsy is an increasingly common finding. Athlete's heart changes can overlap with cardiomyopathy and channelopathy findings, and the review describes ECG and imaging features that help separate them. Compulsory screening in Veneto, Italy, was linked to an 89% fall in incidence in one account, while a study in Israel, based on newspaper reports, found no reduction. The review also notes that recent guidelines take a more liberal, shared decision making approach to exercise in several cardiac conditions.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, and the review relies on heterogeneous definitions and case ascertainment. The authors note that autopsy rates are declining and that some cohorts underestimate events. Evidence on the effects of intense exercise in people with cardiac disease is mainly from retrospective or observational studies, and the authors call for randomised trials.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a holistic assessment combining personal and family history, ECG and imaging before clearing an athlete, and recognise that many cardiac findings are physiological. Keep resuscitation readiness high, with trained staff, a plan and access to an automated external defibrillator, and discuss exercise limits with the athlete and team physician when a condition is found.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Expect endurance and explosive-sport athletes to show heart changes that can overlap with cardiomyopathy, and route equivocal ECG or imaging findings for second-line cardiac investigation rather than assuming disease or normality. Keep emergency action plans and defibrillator access in place through the season.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review summarises guideline recommendations on sports participation after a cardiac diagnosis, such as cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, and recommends shared decision making; it notes athletes with myocarditis should refrain from intense exercise for at least 3 months. It does not provide a return-to-play protocol after cardiac arrest, and the authors note the evidence on high-intensity exercise is limited.

records.sourceFile: Superior labrum anterior-posterior      tears in the NFL.pdf

paper.citation: Chambers CC, Lynch TS, Gibbs DB, Ghodasra JH, Sahota S, Franke K, et al. Superior Labrum Anterior-Posterior Tears in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2017;45(1):167.
paper.abstract: The authors analysed SLAP tears in NFL players using league injury surveillance data from 2000 to 2014 and Scouting Combine records from 2003 to 2011. SLAP tears were a small share of shoulder injuries, surgically treated tears caused much more time lost, and Combine athletes with prior repair who were drafted had fewer games played and started.
paper.tldr: SLAP tears are uncommon in NFL players but cost substantial time when they need surgery. Players with a prior SLAP repair who were drafted played noticeably fewer games than matched peers.
paper.methods: Two-part descriptive study. NFL Injury Surveillance System records of SLAP tears from 2000 to 2014 were analysed by position, play type, days and games lost and surgery. Scouting Combine athletes from 2003 to 2011 with a prior SLAP repair were identified from medical evaluations and compared with matched drafted controls on career length and performance score. Groups were compared with t tests and chi-square tests.
paper.findings: SLAP tears were 3.1% of NFL shoulder injuries (65 cases), most often in offensive linemen (27.7%), and about two-thirds occurred in games. Surgical treatment (41.5% of cases) was associated with more days missed (140.2 vs 21.5, P < .001) and games missed (8.4 vs 2.6, P = .003) than nonoperative care. Of 2,965 Combine athletes, 25 reported a prior SLAP repair; 18 of them were drafted, and compared with 18 matched controls they had similar performance scores (3.63 for both) and years played (3.4 vs 4.0, P = .063), but fewer games played (33.7 vs 48.3, P = .049) and games started (19.6 vs 35.4, P = .036).
paper.limitations: Small sample sizes and possible underreporting of less severe injuries, particularly in Combine self-reported history. The surveillance system did not record SLAP subtype, injury severity or surgical detail, so the time-loss comparison may reflect severity. Estimated return dates were included in days missed, and career statistics came from unofficial public sources. The authors call for confirmation in larger populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat a SLAP tear in a contact athlete as a potentially career-affecting injury and plan for substantial time lost if surgery is needed. Three quarters of in-game SLAP tears occurred during contact with another player, most commonly while tackling or blocking, so the mechanism and play type are worth recording when a contact athlete presents with shoulder symptoms. The study did not test any prevention or treatment strategy.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Track shoulder surgical history at the Combine and in medical screening, since drafted players with a prior SLAP repair played and started fewer games than matched controls despite similar draft rates and performance scores. Expect linemen to be the most often affected, as offensive linemen had the most SLAP tears in both the NFL and Combine groups.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Surgically treated SLAP tears in NFL players were followed by a mean of 140 days missed compared with about three weeks for nonoperative management, which gives a rough time-loss benchmark. The study does not measure return to prior performance level after surgery, so it cannot guide return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Systematic review of pre-injury migraines as a vulnerability factor for worse outcome following sport-related concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Terry DP, Büttner F, Huebschmann NA, Gardner AJ, Cook NE, Iverson GL. Systematic Review of Pre-injury Migraines as a Vulnerability Factor for Worse Outcome Following Sport-Related Concussion. Frontiers in Neurology. 2022;13:915357.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 27 studies asked whether pre-injury migraine is associated with slower recovery after sport-related concussion. Most studies found no association, and the authors judge the evidence to suggest, but not prove, that pre-injury migraine may be a vulnerability factor.
paper.tldr: Most studies found no link between a pre-injury migraine history and slower concussion recovery, but the largest and best-designed studies hint at a higher risk in a subgroup of athletes. Staff should treat a migraine history as a possible risk marker to monitor, not a confirmed predictor.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol. Searches of nine databases covered English-language studies to 15 May 2021, and studies of pre-injury migraine as a predictor of sport-related concussion recovery were included. Risk of bias was rated with QUIPS, levels of evidence with OCEBM, and a likelihood-ratio heuristic was used to summarize the mixed results without meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Across 25 unique samples, 8,692 athletes had sport-related concussion and at least 1,015 had pre-injury migraine history (11.8%). Nineteen studies found no significant association with recovery, two had mixed findings, and four reported only positive findings, with six of 25 studies showing at least one significant result. In a prospective high school and college cohort (117 athletes with migraine), a lower share of migraine athletes had returned to school at 7, 14 and 21 days, with no difference in return to play. In a large emergency department cohort, 42.6% of youth with migraine versus 28.1% without had symptoms at 28 days (multivariable OR 1.73). The likelihood ratio at 80% power and alpha 0.05 favored the null for all studies (429,001) but favored the alternative for studies with 50 or more migraine participants (8.05, weak to moderate).
paper.limitations: Pre-injury migraine was assessed by single self-report items in most studies, with little information on age of onset, frequency or treatment. Most studies were rated moderate risk of bias, many had fewer than 20 migraine participants, outcomes and time points varied, and confounding by sex and prior concussion was rarely handled. The authors also note that only published studies were included, so publication bias is possible.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can ask every athlete about pre-injury migraine history at baseline and after concussion, and consider it alongside other risk markers. The review does not support a specific monitoring threshold or a change in management for athletes with migraines.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review does not study training, performance or load. Its relevance is to baseline screening, because athletes with migraines have been reported to show more symptoms and vestibular or ocular-motor provocation at preseason baseline testing, which can affect how baselines are interpreted.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review suggests a subgroup of athletes with pre-injury migraine may take longer to recover, with one large cohort showing more symptoms at 28 days, but most studies found no difference in return to play. It cannot set return-to-play criteria, and it should not be used to delay or accelerate clearance for an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Tackle characteristics associated with concussion in elite men's rugby union - Unpicking the differences between tacklers and ball-carriers.pdf

paper.citation: Stokes KA, Locke D, Roberts S, et al. Tackle characteristics associated with concussion in elite men's rugby union: unpicking the differences between tacklers and ball-carriers. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2025;11:e002612.
paper.abstract: The authors identified tackle characteristics associated with concussion for tacklers and ball-carriers in five seasons of English Premiership rugby union, using a case-control design. Of 231 video-identified concussions, 178 occurred to tacklers and 53 to ball-carriers, and these were compared with 9,963 control tackles. Lower tackles reduced the odds of concussion to ball-carriers, while the odds for tacklers were more nuanced but relatively low when contact was made with the ball-carrier's torso.
paper.tldr: In elite rugby union, contacting the ball-carrier's torso carried relatively low concussion odds for both players, while head or neck contact with the ball-carrier was linked to high odds. Lower tackle height appears to reduce concussion risk for ball-carriers, but the tackler results are more mixed.
paper.methods: Case-control study of male professional players in The English Premiership (2016/2017 to 2020/2021). Concussion cases were video-coded from club-reported events, and each was compared with control tackles from the same fixtures (25 tackles before and after the event). A random forest selected key variables, and generalised linear mixed models with player as a random effect estimated odds ratios with 90% CIs.
paper.findings: For tacklers, every head-contact location raised odds versus no head contact; head-to-torso raised them about 6.5-fold (OR 6.5, 90% CI 4.0 to 10.7) and was among the lowest of the head-contact categories, and head-to-knee had the highest odds (OR 155.8, 90% CI 75.3 to 322.4). Head-to-hip occurred most often and had the highest number of concussions per 1,000 tackles (3.1). For ball-carriers, head-to-head contact had the highest odds (OR 104.3, 90% CI 56.7 to 192.0), and first contact to the head or neck had higher odds than torso contact (OR 27.2, 90% CI 15.2 to 48.7). The authors report that the random forest models had AUROC values of 0.73 to 0.84.
paper.limitations: Only 54% of reported concussions could be identified on video, and ball-carrier events were harder to identify, which may bias the tackler-versus-ball-carrier comparison. The sample was small once several characteristics were combined, so interaction estimates are imprecise. Results come from one league over five seasons, and the 90% CIs are wide for several contact categories. The ball-carrier head and neck versus torso OR is printed with two different CIs (15.2 to 48.7 and 13.6 to 54.5).
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and policy makers can use the finding that torso contact carries lower concussion odds for both players, supporting tackle-height strategies that target the torso. Tackle coaching could also address head contact with a ball-carrier's hip or knee and with a teammate's head, which had higher odds for tacklers.
paper.athleteDev: Tackle training can focus on initial contact with the ball-carrier's torso and on keeping the tackler's head away from the ball-carrier's hip, knee and a teammate's head. Very low tackles that brought the tackler's head onto the ball-carrier's knee had high odds, and an upright tackler making first contact with the ball-carrier's head or neck had higher tackler odds than upright contact to the torso, so body position and contact height are both training targets.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study describes tackle characteristics associated with concussion occurrence and does not assess recovery, return-to-play timing or post-concussion management.

records.sourceFile: Tackle techniques and characteristics associated with a concussion in tackling players in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Sherwood CP, Grogan F, McMurry TL, et al. Tackle techniques and characteristics associated with a concussion in tackling players in the National Football League. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: The authors reviewed video of 51 NFL tackler concussions from the 2015 to 2019 seasons and 96 matched control tackles, coding 20 technique variables. Closing speed was significantly associated with concussion in every model, and the tackler leading with the helmet, helmet as primary contact or loading, and head placement across the ball carrier's path had the largest associations. Torso as the ball carrier's primary loading area had the lowest risk.
paper.tldr: Tacklers who led with the helmet, took the main load on the helmet, or placed their head across the ball carrier's path had higher concussion odds in matched NFL tackles. Coaching players to target the torso and keep their head on the correct side may lower risk, although closing speed was the strongest factor.
paper.methods: Matched case-control study using a qualitative video review of 1-on-1 pass and rush tackles. Each concussion case was matched to 1 to 3 control tackles using Next Gen Stats trajectory and closing speed, and 20 technique variables were coded for both groups. Conditional logistic regression adjusted for closing velocity, with false discovery rate correction across models.
paper.findings: Tacklers who led with the helmet had an OR of 5.18 (95% CI 1.87 to 14.33), and helmet as primary loading had an OR of 4.61 (95% CI 1.41 to 15.05). Head placed across the ball carrier's path had an OR of 4.17 (95% CI 1.58 to 11.01) relative to head on the correct side, and a shoulder initial contact had an OR of 0.17 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.78) relative to helmet. Each 1 m/s increase in closing speed was associated with a roughly tenfold increase in risk, and ball-carrier torso loading had the lowest risk of the body parts coded.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, with 51 cases and 96 controls, and several variables produced undefined or very wide odds ratios. Controls were matched on tracking data and closing speed, not on full kinematics, and the authors note that some variables were correlated with each other. The study was funded by the NFL, and the author list includes an NFL employee and authors with consulting ties to the NFL.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can teach tacklers to keep the helmet out of the tackle, to place the head on the correct side of the ball carrier, and to target the torso, all of which were linked to lower concussion odds in this sample. Closing speed had the most consistent association, but the authors' recommendations focus on helmet involvement, head placement and torso targeting rather than on speed.
paper.athleteDev: Technique training can focus on minimising helmet involvement, placing the head outside the ball carrier's path, and aiming for the torso. Shortening steps, bending at the waist and use of the arms were not significantly associated with tackler concussion in this NFL sample, unlike earlier rugby findings.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study examines tackle technique and concussion occurrence in NFL games and does not assess recovery, return-to-play decisions or post-concussion management.

records.sourceFile: Tackler and ball carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries compared with player-matched and team-matched injury free controls in elite Rugby Union.pdf

paper.citation: Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.
paper.tldr: Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.
paper.methods: Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5. A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.
paper.findings: For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. For upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact, injured front-on tacklers scored lower than team controls in both their injury and own-control tackles, which the authors read as an existing deficit in these players rather than a lapse during the injury event.
paper.limitations: The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries only 108 were identified on video and 74 met the criteria for analysis. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers. The authors suggest building team databases of technique scores to find individual deficits.
paper.athleteDev: The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper.

records.sourceFile: Tacklers' head inertial accelerations can be decreased by alterning the way they engage in contact with ball carriers torsos.pdf

paper.citation: Edwards S, Gardner A, Tahu T, et al. Tacklers' Head Inertial Accelerations Can Be Decreased by Altering the Way They Engage in Contact with Ball Carriers' Torsos. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: The authors used 3D motion capture to examine how four legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles affected the head kinematics of tacklers and ball carriers, using 455 successful trials from 15 rugby players. Tackles differed in the height of contact on the ball carrier's torso and in the tackler's technique. The tackler had the highest peak head accelerations when contacting the lower torso, and a modified smother tackle reduced tackler linear head acceleration compared with the traditional upper-torso smother.
paper.tldr: In a lab study of slow front-on tackles, contacting the hip area produced the highest tackler head accelerations, while a modified smother tackle with a pop-and-lock action produced lower tackler linear head acceleration. Mid-torso contact may lower tackler head loads, but it shifts more load to the ball carrier.
paper.methods: Laboratory experimental study with a within-player design. Fifteen healthy male rugby players, paired in sessions, each completed 10 trials of each of four tackle instructions (dominant NRL, dominant torso and stick, smother NRL, and smother ball pop and lock) at 80% game intensity, with roles reversed. Full-body 3D motion capture (300 Hz) was used, and mixed general linear models compared peak resultant linear and angular head accelerations across instructions.
paper.findings: For tacklers, the dominant NRL (hip-area) tackle produced significantly higher peak linear and angular head accelerations than the other three instructions (linear p less than 0.001 against each; angular p of 0.013 or lower against each). The smother ball, pop and lock tackle had lower tackler linear head acceleration than the smother NRL and dominant torso and stick tackles (p = 0.001 each); in the Table 2 post hoc tests, tackler angular acceleration differed only between the hip-area tackle and the others. For ball carriers, the dominant NRL tackle produced the smallest peak linear and angular head accelerations, and the pop-and-lock tackle produced higher ball-carrier accelerations than the smother NRL and dominant torso and stick tackles.
paper.limitations: The abstract says mid and upper torso tackles produced the lowest ball-carrier head kinematics, but the results and discussion say the hip-area tackle did, so this report follows the results. The results text also says the pop-and-lock tackle lowered tackler angular acceleration versus two other tackles, but Table 2 and the discussion show angular differences only for the hip-area tackle. The study had 15 players, slow tackles, no ground contact, one expert coach, and 145 of 600 trials removed as unsuccessful, which may bias the findings. Injury history was not recorded, and the authors note that the behaviour change was tested only in one session.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can consider mid-torso contact as a target for dominant tackles, since the hip-area tackle gave the highest tackler head accelerations in this lab setting. The authors note a trade-off, because the ball carrier's head loads rise with higher contact, so the change needs testing in match conditions before it is adopted.
paper.athleteDev: The lower-acceleration modified tackles were performed with less head flexion and a straighter back than the standard NRL tackles, and in the pop-and-lock variant the head was placed outside the ball carrier's shoulder. These features were not tested on their own, and the results come from slow, expert-coached trials that did not go to ground.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study measures head kinematics in healthy players during slow simulated tackles and does not assess concussion, recovery or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Tendon and Ligament Injuries in   Elite Rugby- The Potential Genetic Influence.pdf

paper.citation: Brazier J, Antrobus M, Stebbings GK, Day SH, Heffernan SM, Cross MJ, et al. Tendon and ligament injuries in elite rugby: The potential genetic influence. Sports. 2019;7:138.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises tendon and ligament injury incidence and severity in elite rugby union and rugby league and discusses tendon and ligament biology and possible genetic influences on injury. It proposes nine candidate genes for study in elite rugby and other invasion sports.
paper.tldr: Tendon and ligament injuries are among the most frequent and severe in elite rugby, and genetic variation may partly explain why some players are more susceptible. The genetic link is not yet proven and the candidate genes need testing in large elite cohorts.
paper.methods: Narrative review. A structured literature search used terms on elite rugby injury, injury mechanisms, tendon and ligament epidemiology, pathophysiology and genetics, and reference lists of the articles found were checked. Databases, dates and inclusion criteria are not reported.
paper.findings: The authors report that rugby union has one of the highest reported injury incidences of professional sport and that tendon and ligament injuries are among the most severe. They describe the biology of tendons and ligaments and summarise evidence that genetic variation may influence injury susceptibility, but they state that much stronger evidence is needed. They propose nine candidate genes (COL1A1, COL3A1, COL5A1, MIR608, MMP3, TIMP2, VEGFA, NID1, COLGALT1) for study in elite rugby.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no reported search databases, dates or quality appraisal. The genetic evidence is limited and largely from candidate-gene studies. The authors note that very large samples, probably hundreds or thousands of players, would be needed for genetic studies in elite sport.
paper.practicalImplications: Genetic markers are not ready for use in selecting or managing players. The authors suggest that genetic analysis of players already in large rugby injury databases could show whether the proposed genes relate to injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: This paper does not provide a training or performance method. It identifies tendon and ligament injury as a major concern in rugby and proposes genetic research that may later inform individual load and injury-risk management.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It contains no return-to-play outcomes, rehabilitation data or clinical criteria, and its genetic markers are not validated for prognosis.

records.sourceFile: The Association Between Central Nervous System Function and Core Body Temperature in Patients With Exertional Heat Stroke.pdf

paper.citation: Yeargin SW, Scarneo-Miller SE, Jardine J, Troyanos C, Lopez R. The Association Between Central Nervous System Function and Core Body Temperature in Patients With Exertional Heat Stroke. Clin J Sport Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: The study describes central nervous system function using the Glasgow Coma Scale in patients with exertional heat stroke treated at a road race medical tent, and tests whether GCS relates to rectal temperature. The authors find only a weak overall correlation and none above 40 C, and conclude that GCS may not capture CNS dysfunction in this condition.
paper.tldr: In 25 runners treated for exertional heat stroke, Glasgow Coma Scale scores tracked rectal temperature only weakly and not at the dangerous high temperatures. Rectal temperature should still guide cooling, and mental status alone should not be used to stop it.
paper.methods: Retrospective cross-sectional review of deidentified medical charts from an 11 km race medical tent. Scribes recorded GCS subscales and cumulative scores at each rectal temperature reading, roughly every 3 minutes, and Spearman correlations tested the link between rectal temperature and GCS in the 22 patients with at least one documented GCS score.
paper.findings: Of 25 patients (14 men, 11 women, aged 29 plus or minus 13 years), the mean initial rectal temperature was 41.0 plus or minus 0.6 C and the mean cumulative GCS was 14 plus or minus 3 (range 4 to 15). Confusion was the most frequently recorded CNS sign (19.8%). Overall, rectal temperature and GCS had a significant but weak negative correlation (rs = -0.255, p = 0.004, R2 = 0.06). At time points above 40 C, the correlation was not significant (rs = -0.209, p = 0.108), and the Eye, Verbal and Motor subscales were also not significant.
paper.limitations: Charts were completed during busy care, so some variables were not recorded at every time point, and persistent signs were not always documented. Only patients who reached a station with their own chart were included. The study is from one race with 25 patients, and the authors say a universal GCS guideline cannot be drawn from it.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians should keep using rectal temperature to guide cold water immersion and to decide when to stop cooling, and should not use GCS or mental status to decide when cooling is complete. Where rectal temperature cannot be measured, the authors suggest estimating cooling time from the likely core temperature, the body area in water and the water temperature, while noting this does not represent best practice.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study concerns acute heat illness rather than performance. For staff at endurance events, it reinforces that rectal temperature measurement should be available at the medical tent.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper covers acute treatment of exertional heat stroke in race patients and does not address return to sport. It cannot inform return timing or criteria after heat stroke.

records.sourceFile: The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Chundi G, Dawar A, Fuller Z, Jones T, Lingam S, Galdi B. The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2026;26:e70120.
paper.abstract: The study tested whether playing only football in high school is associated with higher injury rates and shorter NFL careers than multisport participation. Among NFL draftees from 2011 to 2023, multisport athletes had fewer total and major injuries per 1000 snaps and longer careers.
paper.tldr: Among NFL draftees, those who played several sports in high school had fewer injuries per snap and longer careers than those who played only football. The result is an association from observational data, so it does not show that early specialization causes harm.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort of NFL players drafted 2011 to 2023 who played at least 16 career games, excluding kickers and punters. High school sport history came from public records and injury data from online databases. Injury rates per 1000 snaps were compared using position-stratified incidence rate ratios, with false discovery rate correction for position analyses. Concussions, illnesses, upper extremity fractures and jaw or facial fractures were excluded from the injury counts, and multisport status meant at least one other varsity sport in grades 9 to 12.
paper.findings: Of 2,556 players, about 64% were multisport athletes. Multisport athletes had lower total injury incidence (IRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.85) and major injury incidence (IRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.82), both p less than 0.001. They played 12.2 more NFL games (95% CI 9.2 to 15.1) and had 0.7 more career years (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9). By position, lower injury rates in multisport athletes remained significant after false discovery rate correction for defensive backs, defensive linemen, linebackers, running backs and wide receivers, but not for offensive linemen, quarterbacks or tight ends.
paper.limitations: The retrospective design cannot establish causation, and the authors note that athleticism or coaching quality could explain both specialization and durability. Classification and injury reporting may be incomplete, minor in-play injuries were not captured, and models were not adjusted for age or other player characteristics. The cohort is male, elite and drafted only, and the authors note that definitions of early specialization vary across the literature. Classification used high school participation only, so specialization before age 14 could not be identified, and the authors note their definition aligns with what other studies call later specialization.
paper.practicalImplications: Youth football programmes and families can use these results to support multisport participation in high school, since the study links it with fewer injuries and longer careers. Staff should not use the result to claim that early football specialization directly causes injury, because the study cannot separate it from athlete and coaching differences.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings support encouraging young football players to take part in other sports, since multisport history was linked with longer professional careers and more games played. The study does not measure performance itself.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study covers injury incidence and career length in professional players, not rehabilitation or return from a specific injury. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The Athlete's Heart - Allometric considerations on published papers and relation to cardiovascular variables.pdf

paper.citation: Sejersen C, Volianitis S, Secher NH. The athlete's heart: allometric considerations on published papers and relation to cardiovascular variables. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.
paper.abstract: The authors pooled left ventricular dimensions from published studies of male endurance athletes, weightlifters and untrained controls, scaled to body weight. Left ventricular internal diameter tracked stroke volume, cardiac output and blood volume, while wall thickness did not track these variables.
paper.tldr: Among male athletes, the enlarged chamber size of the heart is linked to stroke volume and blood volume, while wall thickness is not. Heart size comparisons between sports should be scaled to body weight.
paper.methods: The authors searched PubMed to April 2022 and added references from prior papers, and included male athletes aged 18 to 40 in endurance sports and weightlifting, with untrained controls. Left ventricular and atrial dimensions and cardiovascular variables were allometrically scaled to body weight and compared with one-way Welch ANOVA, and correlations were tested with Pearson's r. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, though a search and pooled analysis were carried out.
paper.findings: The search yielded 150 included studies, with 927 athletes and 173 controls. With scaling to body weight, left ventricular internal diameter was similar in weightlifters and controls and 7% to 15% larger in the other athletic groups, while wall thickness was 9% to 24% larger in all athletes. Internal diameter correlated with stroke volume, oxygen pulse, maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac output and blood volume (r about 0.9), and wall thickness did not correlate with these variables.
paper.limitations: The heart and exercise data often come from different populations, and the cross-sectional measures at rest may not reflect sport-specific values. Posture and movement artefacts limit exercise measurements, disciplines within a sport were not separated, and scaling used group means rather than individual values. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, but it also pooled data from a described PubMed search.
paper.practicalImplications: When comparing heart dimensions across athletes of different body sizes, scale the values to body weight. The pooled data link a larger chamber diameter to blood volume and stroke volume, while the authors propose, without direct evidence here, that a thicker wall reflects the pressure needed to drive the enlarged chamber.
paper.athleteDev: The paper gives context for the typical group-level heart size pattern across endurance sports and weightlifting in male athletes. The pooled group means are not individual reference norms and should not be used to judge a single athlete's heart.
paper.rtp: The paper studies healthy male athletes and does not address injury, cardiac pathology or return to sport. It cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to sport or to judge cardiac risk.

records.sourceFile: The Dose–Response Relationship of Exercise-Based Injury Prevention Programmes - Implications for Research and Practice.pdf

paper.citation: Iatropoulos S, Dandrieux PE, Navarro L, Blanco D, Edouard P. The Dose-Response Relationship of Exercise-Based Injury Prevention Programmes: Implications for Research and Practice. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: Exercise-based injury prevention programmes need a period of consistent practice before they reduce injury risk. The authors explain the dose-response concept from pharmacology, show that most RCTs analyse injuries from the first day of the programme, and illustrate two statistical approaches that remove early injuries from the analysis.
paper.tldr: Injury prevention programmes take weeks to work, so analysing injuries from day one can hide their effect. Plan start dates well before the period when protection is needed.
paper.methods: Narrative Current Opinion. The authors outline dose-response concepts, screen the sport RCTs in six recent systematic reviews without a systematic search protocol, and re-analyse one earlier athletics RCT using two approaches.
paper.findings: Of 36 screened RCTs, 33 (92%) did not account for dilution, re-injury or interaction effects, and three accounted for dilution only. In the athletics example, the odds ratio for weekly injury prevalence was 0.85 (0.67-1.09) in the primary analysis, 0.75 (0.56-1.01) after excluding the early period, 0.37 (0.25-0.55) with the inclusion approach and 0.28 (0.16-0.48) with the exclusion approach. The authors estimate that about 6 weeks were needed before this programme reached full effect. In the van der Horst Nordic hamstring trial, cited by the authors, the prevalence reduction was 67% for weeks 14-52 but 56% over the full 52 weeks.
paper.limitations: The authors call the approaches promising but untested in other RCTs, and the screen was not systematic. Most worked examples come from a single trial.
paper.practicalImplications: Start a prevention block several weeks before the period it should protect. Do not judge a programme by injuries that occur in its first weeks, and keep athletes on the programme after an early injury.
paper.athleteDev: Start the injury prevention block several weeks before the competition period it is meant to protect, and keep training through an early injury, because the programme is still building its effect. This is a planning point, not a training-adaptation finding.
paper.rtp: Not a return-to-sport study. It does not test rehabilitation, return criteria or re-injury after return, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines; the timing point applies only to prevention programmes.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of Bye Weeks on Injury Event Rates in the Canadian Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Lee C, Batomen B, Naidu D, Hoeber S, McCormack R, Steele R, et al. The Effect of Bye Weeks on Injury Event Rates in the Canadian Football League. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Retrospective cohort of CFL regular-season games from 2011 to 2018 testing whether a bye week changes the game injury event rate in the following week. The rate after a bye week did not differ meaningfully from non-bye weeks, and adding more bye weeks did not change that.
paper.tldr: Bye weeks did not lower the CFL game injury rate in the following week or in the two or three weeks after. Recorded injuries rose once practice injuries were included, which the authors suggest reflects players being cleared to return rather than new injury.
paper.methods: Historical cohort using the CFL injury surveillance database and official schedules for the 2011 to 2018 regular seasons, with preseason and playoff games excluded. Game injury incidence rate ratios were estimated with conditional quasi-Poisson regression, adjusted for game number, opponent, home or away, and team-year, with a lagged deviance residual term for autocorrelation.
paper.findings: The primary IRR was 0.96 (0.87 to 1.05), and sensitivity analyses that used only the three pre-bye weeks as controls showed no reduction. Cumulative IRRs were 1.02 for two weeks and 1.00 for three weeks, and results were similar with one, two or three bye weeks. Adding practice injuries, the week-after-bye IRR was 1.14 (1.05 to 1.23), which the authors attribute to medical clearance for pre-existing injuries being recorded as new injuries.
paper.limitations: Injury data were collected for clinical documentation rather than research, and the authors could not evaluate coaching or injury-reporting decisions. Practice exposure was not counted, and the residual time-trend confounding the authors note in their sensitivity analyses means the primary estimate should be read with caution.
paper.practicalImplications: On this evidence, a bye week is not a tool for reducing game injuries in the CFL. Injury charting rules for new versus recurring injuries should be consistent, because the authors say the combined result depends on that distinction.
paper.athleteDev: Bye weeks did not change game injury incidence in this sample, so any performance case for them rests on other effects such as rest and preparation time, which the authors discuss but did not measure. The authors suggest the first practices after a bye could be eased in case of deconditioning, but this was not tested.
paper.rtp: The study does not measure return-to-play timing, re-injury or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions after a bye week.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of Sport Specialization on Injury Risk in NCAA Athletes - Results From the SAFE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: Lutsic JJ, Lutsic SE, Ibrahim DS, Augusta MC, Robinson JD, Tong KM, et al. The Effect of Sport Specialization on Injury Risk in NCAA Athletes: Results From the SAFE Consortium. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Retrospective cohort of 211 NCAA athletes who completed a questionnaire on sport specialization and injury history. Highly specialized athletes reported more injuries, more upper and lower extremity injuries and more surgery than low specialized athletes.
paper.tldr: In this NCAA sample, athletes classed as highly specialized reported more injuries, more upper and lower limb injuries and more surgery than low specialized athletes. The data are self-reported and retrospective, so use this as a reason to review training variety, not as proof of cause.
paper.methods: An anonymous questionnaire was completed by collegiate athletes from Division I, II and III schools in the SAFE Consortium during the 2022 to 2023 school year. Specialization was classed low, moderate or high on a 3-point scale (single-sport focus, quitting other sports, year-round training), and injuries were grouped as upper or lower extremity, analyzed with chi-square tests and ANOVA.
paper.findings: Of 211 completers, 157 (74.4%) reported an injury, and highly specialized athletes were more likely than low specialized athletes to report any injury (chi-square 19.81, P<0.0001). High specialization was associated with more upper extremity injuries (chi-square 7.17, P=0.007), lower extremity injuries (chi-square 4.11, P=0.04) and surgery (chi-square 6.76, P=0.009). Moderate specialization was associated with more lower extremity injuries (P=0.03) but not upper extremity injuries (P=0.052), and average days away from sport were 85 for low, 110 for moderate and 112 for high specialization, with no statistical test reported for the days.
paper.limitations: Injuries were self-reported with recall bias, the questionnaire is not fully validated, and athletes reported injuries from both before and after NCAA registration, so the injury history spans youth sport. The abstract reports P<0.0001 for upper and lower extremity injuries, but the Results give P=0.007 and P=0.04; the Results values are reported here. Days away from sport were compared without a reported test, and the design is retrospective and cross-sectional in effect.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend educating athletes, parents and coaches about the link between high specialization and upper and lower extremity injuries, periodizing training and competition, monitoring for overuse signs and encouraging cross-training. These recommendations follow from the association, but this study did not test them.
paper.athleteDev: Highly specialized athletes in this sample reported more injuries and more days away from practice and competition, so training variety and planned rest are reasonable topics for athlete development plans. The study does not show how much specialization is safe, or whether cross-training reduces risk.
paper.rtp: Days away from sport were longer for highly specialized athletes (112 versus 85 days), but these are self-reported durations with no reported statistical test, and the study does not follow injured athletes through rehabilitation, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of the Number of Carries on Injury Risk and Subsequent Season’s Performance Among Running Backs in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Kraeutler MJ, Belk JW, McCarty EC. The Effect of the Number of Carries on Injury Risk and Subsequent Season's Performance Among Running Backs in the National Football League. Orthop J Sports Med. 2017;5(2):2325967117691941.
paper.abstract: Retrospective cohort of 275 NFL running back player-seasons from 2004 to 2014, comparing players with 150 to 250 carries and players with 300 or more carries. Players with fewer carries missed more games to injury the following season, and yards per carry did not differ significantly between groups.
paper.tldr: High-carry running backs in this NFL sample did not show more injury or lower yards per carry the following season, and they missed fewer games than moderate-carry backs. Carry totals alone should not be used to predict next-season injury risk for running backs.
paper.methods: ESPN NFL statistics and team injury reports were used for running backs with 150 to 250 carries (group A) or 300 or more carries (group B) in each regular season from 2004 to 2014; players with 251 to 299 carries were excluded. Changes between seasons within each group were tested with matched-pair t tests, between-group differences with t tests, and missed-game categories with chi-square tests.
paper.findings: Group A missed more games in the season of interest (1.86 vs 0.19) and in the following season (3.27 vs 1.89), and a higher share of group A missed at least one game the next season (66% vs 49%, P=0.016). Yards per carry did not differ between groups in the preceding season (P=0.073) or the next season (P=0.24), and carries fell in both groups the next season. Overall, 62% of the running backs missed at least one game the next season, with concussion the most common cause of missed time.
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective and depends on the accuracy of NFL game summaries and injury reports, and some players appear in more than one season, so the 275 player-seasons come from about 128 different players. Play-call distribution, offensive philosophy, line performance, opponent quality and weather were not controlled, and short receptions that count as running plays were not captured. The authors also note that yards per carry may be a weak measure of running back performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Carry totals alone did not predict next-season injury or yards per carry in this sample, so workload decisions for running backs should use more than carry counts. According to the authors, running backs as a group had high missed-time rates regardless of carry totals.
paper.athleteDev: For performance planning, carry volume did not explain next-season missed games or yards per carry in this sample, so carry counts should not be the sole basis for a running back's load plan. Carry totals fell for both groups the next season, partly because of rookies and multi-back offenses, the authors suggest, which limits what carry data can say about workload.
paper.rtp: The study counts games missed in a season, not rehabilitation time or return to play after a specific injury, so it cannot set return-to-play timing for running backs.

records.sourceFile: The Epidemiology of Ankle Injuries Identified at the National Football League Combine, 2009-2015.pdf

paper.citation: Mulcahey MK, Bernhardson AS, Murphy CP, Chang A, Zajac T, Sanchez G, et al. The Epidemiology of Ankle Injuries Identified at the National Football League Combine, 2009-2015. Orthop J Sports Med. 2018;6(7):2325967118786227.
paper.abstract: Retrospective chart review of ankle injuries in 2,285 players at the 2009 to 2015 NFL Combine. Over half had a history of ankle injury, sprains were the most common type, and the proportion with injury varied by position, highest in running backs, offensive linemen and tight ends.
paper.tldr: Over half of invited NFL Combine players had a past ankle injury, mostly sprains, and running backs, linemen and tight ends had the highest proportions. Use these as prevalence figures for history-taking and clinical awareness, not as injury rates.
paper.methods: Charts of all 2,285 combine participants were reviewed for history, examination findings, radiographs and MRI, with ankle imaging performed in players who reported an ankle injury or had consistent findings. Injury types, locations, osteoarthritis and surgery were tabulated as simple percentages, and position-level injury percentages used all combine players at each position as the denominator (the column totals sum to 2,285, although the table labels them 'with imaging').
paper.findings: Of 1,216 players (53.2%) with an ankle injury, 229 had injuries to both ankles, giving 1,445 injured ankles; sprains were 86.0% of these, and 137 ankle fractures were identified. Among players with radiographs, 611 (50.6%) had ankle osteoarthritis, and cartilage lesions were found on MRI in 69 of the 257 ankles imaged. Running backs (61.9%), offensive linemen (60.3%) and tight ends (59.4%) had the highest proportions with any ankle injury, while kickers (23.3%) and long snappers (37.5%) had the lowest.
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective, and imaging was done only for players with a history or findings, so MRI findings come from about 10% of players. Injury timing was unclear, so acute and remote injuries are mixed, and exposure was not recorded, so injury rates cannot be compared directly with other sports. Physical examination data were incompletely reported, and surgical indications were not recorded.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians evaluating football players should check ankle history, sprain type and early osteoarthritis, because these were common in this group. The authors call for prospective work on how prior injuries affect career length, so this paper alone does not justify a position-specific ankle program.
paper.athleteDev: Prior ankle injury was common in this draft-eligible group and varied by position, so position-aware ankle history is a reasonable starting point for performance and medical planning. The study cannot say whether these injuries affect playing career or performance.
paper.rtp: The study describes injury types and surgery use at the combine, not time to return to play or outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines for ankle injuries.

records.sourceFile: The Evolving Treatment Patterns of                        NCAA Division I Football Players by Orthopaedic Team           Physicians      Over     the     Past Decade, 2008-2016.pdf

paper.citation: Carver TJ, Schrock JB, Kraeutler MJ, McCarty EC. The Evolving Treatment Patterns of NCAA Division I Football Players by Orthopaedic Team Physicians Over the Past Decade, 2008-2016. Sports Health. 2018.
paper.abstract: Survey of NCAA Division I head orthopaedic team physicians in 2008 and 2016 to 2017 on how they treat common football injuries. Preferences changed for ACL graft choice, shoulder stabilization, PCL reconstruction and pregame Toradol use, and physicians became more conservative about ACL return to play.
paper.tldr: Team physicians in NCAA Division I football moved toward patellar tendon grafts, arthroscopic shoulder stabilization and arthroscopic single-bundle PCL reconstruction, and away from pregame Toradol. Use these results as a picture of current practice, since they are opinions rather than outcomes.
paper.methods: The head orthopaedic team physician for each NCAA Division I football team was asked to complete a survey on experience, team coverage and treatment preference for common injuries, sent in 2008 and again between April 2016 and April 2017. Responses were compared with chi-square tests, with P less than 0.05 treated as significant.
paper.findings: Patellar tendon autograft was preferred for ACL reconstruction by 83% in 2016 (67% in 2008), and arthroscopic anterior shoulder stabilization rose from 69% to 93%. Arthroscopic single-bundle PCL reconstruction was preferred by 83% (49% in 2008), and pregame Toradol use fell from 62% to 26%. Physicians also became more conservative on ACL return to play: 51% required 7 months or longer in 2016, compared with 70% who allowed return by 6 months in 2008.
paper.limitations: The results reflect expert opinion rather than clinical outcomes, which the authors name as the main limitation. Response rates were 93% and 90%, and the two surveys were compared across different periods with chi-square tests, so changes in the respondent group could contribute to the differences.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors note that treatment patterns shift over time, so older protocols may need checking against current practice. They attribute the decline in pregame Toradol use partly to NFL Physician Society task force recommendations, though they did not test that link.
paper.athleteDev: The paper has little direct training content. Its relevance for performance staff is that more physicians now clear players after ACL reconstruction at 7 months or longer, which affects how training and competition loads are planned for those players.
paper.rtp: The study reports physicians' preferred return-to-play timelines after ACL reconstruction, shoulder stabilization and fifth metatarsal fixation, but these are opinions and do not show that the timelines are safe or effective. Use it to describe current practice, not to set an individual athlete's clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: The Fragility Index of Risk Factors for Hamstring Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Anthis M, Gourd S, Kim B, Ruddy JD, Whiteley R, Timmins R, et al. The Fragility Index of Risk Factors for Hamstring Injuries. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2024;54(10):672-678.
paper.abstract: Objective: to determine the Fragility Index of hamstring injury risk factors, defined as the minimum number of participants who would need to change classification to make a risk factor statistically non-significant. Design: retrospective secondary data analysis. Methods: studies with 2x2 contingency data for hamstring injury risk factors were recalculated, moving one injured high-risk athlete at a time to the non-injured high-risk group until relative risk was no longer significant. Results: the median Fragility Index was 3 (Q1-Q3 2-6) for all significant risk factors, 3 (2-5) for modifiable and 3 (2-6) for nonmodifiable factors. Conclusion: most statistically significant hamstring injury risk factors are fragile associations.
paper.tldr: Most statistically significant hamstring injury risk factors are fragile: moving about 3 injured high-risk athletes would often remove significance. Treat a single significant factor as preliminary and check the number of injuries behind it before acting.
paper.methods: Systematic searches of eight databases (January 2019 to October 2022) and the 78 articles of a prior hamstring risk-factor review were screened. Forty-one studies with extractable 2x2 data were included, and relative risk with 95% CI was recalculated. Each significant factor was shifted one athlete at a time from the true-positive to the false-positive count until the lower CI reached 1. Risk of bias was rated with QUIPS.
paper.findings: The median Fragility Index across 63 significant factors (of 262 variables reported) was 3 (Q1-Q3 2-6). Modifiable and nonmodifiable factors had medians of 3 (2-5) and 3 (2-6). Prior hamstring injury had a median of 4 (2-7.5) across 12 significant reports, and eccentric strength a median of 3.5 (2.75-4.25) across 8. These are counts of reclassified athletes, not effect sizes.
paper.limitations: Only significant factors were analysed, which may overstate fragility for factors chosen for significance. The Fragility Index was designed for balanced trials and was applied to imbalanced observational data, and continuous variables were split at study-specific cut points. The abstract states that over 35% of all included risk factors had a Fragility Index of 2 or less, whereas the Discussion gives one third of significant risk factors; the Discussion figure is reported here. The corresponding author has financial ties to NordBord (VALD), and studies using that device were included.
paper.practicalImplications: Before acting on a significant hamstring risk factor, check how many athletes would need to change status to remove the result. Where acting is cheap, a fragile finding can still justify a cautious response; where costs are high, wait for replication. Research reports should give the Fragility Index alongside sample size and injury counts.
paper.athleteDev: A single significant hamstring risk factor, such as low eccentric strength or prior hamstring injury, is often fragile, so use it as a prompt to screen rather than a firm training target. Apply the same caution to any factor drawn from a small sample with few injuries.
paper.rtp: It does not address return to sport. The studies concern who gets hamstring injuries, so the results cannot guide return-to-play timing, clearance or decisions after a current injury.
